name: Dandelion
lede: Dandelion is the vivid yellow of the flower's petals, named from the French for lion's tooth.

sections.title: A lion's tooth
sections.body:
Paterson defines dandelion as the vivid yellow of the petals, and traces the word to the French *dent de lion*, lion's tooth [1]. He ties the toothed look to the plant's roots, which is a description rather than a sourced etymology [1]. Paterson ranks it among the yellows with daffodil, cowslip and jonquil [2].

The color has more than one reading. Our library holds this swatch (#FED85D) from Wikipedia and ISCC-NBS block 83, while Ridgway's 1912 plate shows a paler tone (#ECCE88) and the xkcd survey a harder one (#FEDF08) [3]. The Ridgway scan is an aged plate and only approximate [3].

sections.title: The same block as old pigments
sections.body:
ISCC-NBS block 83 gathers a crowd of historical names: auripigmentum, Cassel yellow, Dutch pink and [[maize]] are filed there, and so is the pigment name Chinese yellow [3]. The flower's petal color was grouped with pigments whose makers had no connection to it [3].

Nearby named yellows in our library include [[marigold]] and [[mustard]] [3].

sections.title: What the books say about the plant
sections.body:
Finlay describes a Harris Tweed mill where, in the old days, dyers used natural materials, and in his list magenta came from dandelion, not yellow [4]. The book gives no further detail, so this is one mill's recipe, not a general fact [4].

The artist Derek Jarman remembered a childhood horror of dandelions, with the yellow flowers turning brown in death [5]. It is a darker side of a bright yellow flower [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 26 works [6]. George Dawe's portraits account for three of his 50 works, a rate 55 times the archive's [6]. They include [[painting:commons-Q21722763|Portrait of Ivan Vadbolsky]] and the portrait of Ivan Roeren, both of 1823, and the 1820s are the peak decade [6]. India supplies five hits and the Kalighat school three [6].

The earliest hit is a *Saint Peter* of 1445 [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a match is a screen color [6]. In Google Books the word *dandelion* is present from 1800 and peaks about 2016 [7].
